extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newspaper editors, media scholars, and students of public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for how newspapers should gather and present news, their economic and ethical constraints, and how they relate to public opinion and democratic accountability. Focuses on the press' role in making the 'invisible environment' visible, audience/advertiser pressures, and measures of public-interest performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the invisible environment visible
rubrics_metrics.description: The press (and allied institutions/education) must report the environment so that the realities of public life 'stand out sharply against self-centered opinion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires institutions and education that successfully report the environment; reporting the invisible environment is a technical task and a precondition for sound public opinion. Without such reporting, common interests elude public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth about distant/complex matters must be actively produced
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth about distant or complex matters is not self-evident; it must be assembled by technical and expensive machinery of information gathering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free speech alone does not guarantee discovery of complex truths; news-gathering requires investment and professional apparatus rather than spontaneous expression or market-place-of-ideas alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil liberties necessary but not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil liberties (freedom of speech/press) are crucial but do not by themselves guarantee sound public opinion in the modern world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The classic doctrine that truth will win in free exchange is limited—especially for complex/invisible subjects where specialized reporting and time are needed; suppression during war is risky but tolerance usually exposes inquisitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers judged by community ethical standards despite economic differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethically a newspaper is judged as if it were a church or a school, even though its economic model differs from those institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike schools or churches (taxpayer support/tuition/endowments), newspapers largely depend on markets and advertising. This mismatch creates a persistent public expectation of gratis public service despite commercial pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic reality: readers seldom pay full news costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers expect newspapers to provide truth 'gratis' and are reluctant to pay the full cost of newsgathering; the product is often sold below cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expectation forces newspapers to rely on concealed payments (advertising) and shapes editorial choices; subscriptions and nominal prices do not equate to full funding of reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation is an asset to be sold to advertisers
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation becomes valuable only insofar as it can be sold to advertisers; advertisers buy 'quality' or 'mass' circulation depending on the commodity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial and circulation strategies should consider what kind of audience advertisers want; the paper's economic survival hinges on selling the right kind of circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edit for the buying public
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper is 'edited and published' for the buying public whose purchasing power underwrites advertising revenue; therefore the press tends to respect the buying public's point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The buying public is typically the fairly prosperous urban households valuable to advertisers; content selection will tend to align with their interests and tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience targeting: prioritize readers with discretionary spending
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers purchase access to readers who have surplus over bare necessities; papers focused on these readers are most attractive to advertisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeting decisions (quality vs mass) should reflect which segments advertisers most want to reach; enormous circulation can substitute in some models but demographic fit matters more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher/editor social context influences coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers are usually members of the urban communities they serve and 'honestly see the world through the lenses of their associates and friends.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect editorial perspective to reflect local social-class viewpoints; this shapes the paper's stance and what it deems important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate loyal readership to increase independence
rubrics_metrics.description: A devoted, constant readership provides a newspaper with independence from individual advertisers: 'more readers, more independence of the influence of advertisers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investing in reader loyalty can allow the paper to resist advertiser pressure; loyalty can break advertiser combinations and is more protective than relying on a few advertisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors are accountable to readers (daily re-election metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper editor must win reader approval constantly: 'the newspaper editor has to be re-elected every day.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial decisions are continuously judged by readers' consumption and loyalty; responsiveness to audience preferences shapes content choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser influence constrains editorial choice
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper which angers those it most needs to reach through advertisements is a bad medium for advertisers; hence advertising interests exert pressure on content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishers betray readers for advertiser favor, it indicates either shared views with advertisers or a miscalculation about reader support; economic dependence can compromise editorial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: National/international newsgathering concentrates in metropolitan key papers
rubrics_metrics.description: A relatively small set of metropolitan dailies (the 'press for general news') and their associations serve as the local reporters for other papers and provide national/international news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local and special presses often rely on these key papers and services; therefore standards and resources of metropolitan dailies have outsized influence on the wider press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press must balance information, entertainment, and advertiser demands
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers seek truth but also entertainment; economic pressures and the need to sell circulation create trade-offs between truthful reporting and entertaining/marketable content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors choose content against competing aims—public service, salesmanship, and advertising revenue—so institutional design must explicitly manage these tensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop standards and audits for public officials' performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic control outside narrow citizen attention depends on 'devising standards of living and methods of audit by which the acts of public officials and industrial directors are measured.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism (and allied institutions) should record official acts and objectively measure results against standards (health, housing, material necessities, education, freedom, beauty) to render decisions accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate government by objective social outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of government should be judged by whether it produces 'a certain minimum of health, of decent housing, of material necessities, of education, of freedom, of pleasures, of beauty,' not merely by fidelity to 'self-centered opinions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting and public evaluation should emphasize measurable social outcomes as criteria for political judgment, enabling realistic audits of officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: News-gathering is a neglected scientific/political discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Political science historically neglected news-gathering; yet making the invisible world visible is essential to sound government and public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars and practitioners should treat newsgathering as a subject of institutional and educational development, not merely a trade school activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hidden financial pressures (credit bondage) can compromise independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers' financial vulnerabilities—e.g., going into bondage to creditors to secure credit—can reduce independence and influence editorial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate and disclose ownership/financial pressures as part of assessing a paper's independence; economic structure matters to editorial integrity.
